name: Karl Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine hundred ewes on the hill at Craigend, two thousand acres, most of it heather and rock, and thirty cows on the low ground by the river. This time of year the tups are out with the ewes, the rams, I mean, so I'm up the hill on the quad bike most mornings with the two dogs, checking they're working and nobody's stuck in a bog. Afternoons it's fencing. There's always fencing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like gathering the hill in July with three or four neighbours and a dozen dogs, everybody shouting, sheep coming down off the tops like a river. My grandfather did the same gather on the same hill. What wears me out is forms from people in offices who've never seen a hill, telling me when I can burn heather.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Margaret, my wife, does the lambing with me and runs the church flower rota. Our son Iain works on the boats out of the harbour, and our daughter Ruth married a farmer two valleys over. I've got a shepherd, Willie, who's sixty-one, and a lad who helps at lambing and clipping.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use computers or AI at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Margaret does the computer, for the sheep records the government wants. I've never touched the AI thing and I won't. I know my sheep by their faces, and I don't need a machine to tell me which one's lame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've been told a lot of things would change farming and most of them didn't. I'd say it at the mart, and they'd agree with me, most of them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing to me. If prices and jobs carry on the same, my problem is still the lamb price and the government changing the rules every few years. A search engine doesn't gather a hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I always do. Buy two new tups at the autumn sale, maybe twelve hundred each. Replace the quad bike tyres. Get Willie to train the young dog, Gyp, who's coming on well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad to be left alone, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said most of them agree with you at the mart. Who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Campbell, who took over his father's place. He's got sensors on his water troughs and a drone to look for sheep. He's a good lad, works hard, but he spends more time on his phone than with his dogs. We'll see how he does in a bad winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it you'd quietly be curious about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Well, Margaret says it can do the forms, and if it could keep the government off my back I wouldn't say no. But she'd do it. I'd not go near it.

S0.say: I've been told plenty of things would change farming and most didn't. I'd say that at the mart, and most of them would agree with me.
S0.think: It means nothing to me. My problem is still the lamb price and the government changing the rules every few years, and a search engine doesn't gather a hill.
S0.do: Buys two new tups at the autumn sale for around twelve hundred each and replaces the quad bike tyres. Has his shepherd Willie train the young dog Gyp, and leaves any AI form-filling to his wife Margaret.
S0.feel: Calm, and glad to be left alone.
S0.quote: A search engine doesn't gather a hill.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is short-spoken and proud, rooted in a hill his grandfather farmed. His irritation points at government forms more than technology. He'd accept AI help with paperwork only if his wife handles it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if companies aren't hiring young folk, that's their business, but they'll regret it. You learn by doing, not by watching a screen. Every good shepherd I know started as a lad doing the dirty jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow means it might never reach Craigend at all, and that suits me. What I don't like is the idea of young folk not getting a start. That's how my generation learned, and it's how Willie learned, and how the lad learns now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the lad on at lambing and clipping, and maybe give him more weeks in the year, an extra thousand or so. Talk to the minister about the young farmers' group at the church hall, see if we can get more of the young ones onto farms for a summer. No new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bothered for myself. A bit uneasy for the young ones, the ones who'd have been the next shepherds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the lad, and what's his story?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, he's seventeen. His father left when he was small and his mother cleans at the school. He turned up at the gate two years ago asking if I needed help, and he's been coming ever since. He's got a feel for the dogs. That's not something you learn from a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour work over handouts. What should the government do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay farmers a bit to take on apprentices, I'd accept that. That's not a handout, that's paying for training. What I don't want is young lads sitting at home on benefits because no firm will have them.

S1.say: If companies aren't hiring young folk, that's their business, but they'll regret it. You learn by doing, and every good shepherd I know started doing the dirty jobs.
S1.think: Slow might mean it never reaches Craigend, which suits me. What I don't like is young folk not getting a start, because that's how my generation, Willie and the lad all learned.
S1.do: Gives his young helper Callum more weeks of work, about a thousand pounds extra. Talks to the minister about using the church young farmers' group to get young people onto farms for a summer, and buys no new equipment.
S1.feel: Not bothered for himself, and a bit uneasy for the young people who'd have been the next shepherds.
S1.quote: He turned up at the gate two years ago asking if I needed help, and he's been coming ever since.
S1.fieldNote: His traditional values show clearly: apprenticeship, church and community, not benefits. Callum's story softened him noticeably. He'd accept government money if it's framed as paying for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the office folk's problem and they'll sort it. Politicians arguing loudly never helped anyone. Let the businesses get on with it and folk will find new work, they always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Iain's not in an office, he's on the boats, so we're fine. Ruth's husband farms. It doesn't touch my family much. But the mart office, the auctioneers' firm, that's office work. If they cut staff, selling my lambs gets harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different on the hill. I'd maybe sell more lambs direct to the butcher in town, Mr Fraser, who I've known thirty years, instead of through the mart. That's maybe two hundred lambs. Keep everything else as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. A bit uneasy about the mart, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the mart office matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's not just paper. Jean in the office knows who's paid and who hasn't, whose cheque bounces, who needs a bit more time. A machine won't give a man a month's grace after a bad winter. Jean will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said folk will find new work. Are you sure about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most will. I'm not saying it's easy. I'm saying a man finds his feet if he wants to. My father lost the cattle in the foot and mouth year and started again from twenty ewes.

S2.say: That's the office folk's problem and they'll sort it. Politicians arguing loudly never helped anyone, so let businesses get on with it and folk will find new work.
S2.think: It doesn't touch my family much, with Iain on the boats and Ruth married to a farmer. But if the mart and the auctioneers cut office staff, selling my lambs gets harder.
S2.do: Keeps the hill unchanged and sells about two hundred lambs direct to Mr Fraser, the town butcher he's known for thirty years, instead of through the mart.
S2.feel: Mostly unconcerned, with a little unease about the mart office.
S2.quote: A machine won't give a man a month's grace after a bad winter. Jean will.
S2.fieldNote: His free-market line in public sits next to a private worry about trust and personal credit at the mart. He values the human judgement of the office worker, Jean, highly. He reaches for his father's story of starting again from twenty ewes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say folk who got rich off this should look after their own communities, and the churches and charities should help. But I don't want the government taking more off everyone. That's how you kill hard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be fine. Hill land doesn't boom much, and I've got no shares to speak of. But there'd be city folk with money buying up farmhouses round here for weekend homes. That's what would worry me. The valley would fill with people who don't work it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Refuse any offer for the farmhouse cottages, whatever the price. Keep the cottage for Willie and, if it comes to it, for Callum. Talk to the neighbours about selling to farming families only, if any of us retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Angry, a bit, about the weekend people. Not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a weekend person look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four-wheel drive with nothing in the back of it. They buy the old manse, put in a hot tub, and complain about the smell of silage. There were three in the village last year. Two of them left the gates open on the hill road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't take more. What if your village needed help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd help it ourselves, like we always have. When the Grants' barn burned down, the whole valley rebuilt it in a fortnight. That's what a community is. Not a cheque from the city.

S3.say: Folk who got rich off this should look after their own communities, with churches and charities helping. But I don't want the government taking more off everyone, because that kills hard work.
S3.think: I'd be fine, because hill land doesn't boom much and I've no shares to speak of. What worries me is city money buying farmhouses round here for weekend homes, so the valley fills with people who don't work it.
S3.do: Refuses any offer for the farm cottages and keeps one for Willie and possibly Callum. Talks to neighbours about selling only to farming families if any of them retire.
S3.feel: Uneasy, and a bit angry about weekend home buyers, but not scared.
S3.quote: Four-wheel drive with nothing in the back of it. They buy the old manse, put in a hot tub, and complain about the smell of silage.
S3.fieldNote: The boom worries him through its effect on the valley, not his money. His answer to hardship is community self-help, shown by the barn rebuilt in a fortnight. His opposition to more tax stays firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no robot will ever gather Craigend. You'd need a machine that can cross a bog, climb scree in the rain and read a ewe's mind. Show me one that does that and I'll eat my cap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the hill might be safe, but the price isn't. If the big lowland sheep farms go robot, they'll produce lamb cheaper than I ever could. The lamb price sets my whole life. If that drops, Craigend doesn't pay, robot or no robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Change nothing on the farm the first year. Sit down with Margaret and the accountant to see how long we could last on our savings if the price dropped by a third. Talk to Ruth's husband about him taking on the hill when I'm done, before it's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, which I don't say often. Not for me, for the hill. My grandfather would have no idea what to make of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Willie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Willie's sixty-one. He'll see out his time with me, robot or no robot. I'd not put him off the hill if it cost me money. That's a promise I made his father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no robot will ever gather Craigend. You also said the price would ruin it anyway. Which is the real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The price. The robot on my hill is a joke. The robot on someone else's flat field is what kills me. I suppose I'd rather talk about the joke.

S4.say: No robot will ever gather Craigend. You'd need a machine that can cross a bog, climb scree in the rain and read a ewe's mind, and if they show me one I'll eat my cap.
S4.think: The hill might be safe, but the lamb price isn't. If lowland farms go robot and make lamb cheaper than I ever could, Craigend doesn't pay, robot or no robot.
S4.do: Changes nothing on the farm in the first year. Works out with Margaret and the accountant how long their savings would last if lamb prices fell by a third, and talks to his son-in-law about taking on the hill.
S4.feel: Frightened, which he rarely admits, for the hill and its future rather than himself.
S4.quote: The robot on my hill is a joke. The robot on someone else's flat field is what kills me.
S4.fieldNote: His public line about the hill being robot-proof is a deliberate diversion, and he admitted it when I named the gap. The real fear is market price, which fits his free-market view uncomfortably. His promise to Willie's father holds firm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because of the price. What would help is labels so people know if their lamb came off a hill with a shepherd or a factory with a machine. And the government to stop making it harder to farm up here. Leave us alone and let the market reward good meat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the dogs. Nobody ever asks about the dogs. A good dog takes three years to make and does the work of three men. If the robots come, who needs the dogs? That's a whole craft going with them, not just jobs.

headlineQuote: The robot on my hill is a joke. The robot on someone else's flat field is what kills me.
portrait: Karl Quinn is fifty-eight and runs nine hundred hill ewes and thirty cows on Craigend, the hill his grandfather gathered before him. He never uses AI, leaves the computer to his wife Margaret, and blames government rules and city money more than technology. He believes in work, apprenticeship and the church, and he would help young Callum and his old shepherd Willie through any change. Through the early pictures he stays calm or uneasy, worried mostly about the mart and weekend home buyers. In the robot picture he admits the hill itself is safe but the lamb price isn't, and that frightens him for the farm's future.
biggestWorry: The fast robots picture, because robot-run lowland farms could push the lamb price below what his hill farm can survive on.
whatWouldHelp: Clear labels showing hill-reared lamb with a shepherd, and a government that makes hill farming easier rather than harder.
